passages.happening:
The Pharisees have heard that Jesus is gaining more disciples than John the Baptist. John adds a small correction: Jesus himself did not baptize; his disciples did (verse 2). So Jesus leaves Judea in the south and heads home to Galilee in the north.

“Now He had to pass through Samaria” (verse 4). Samaria was the hill country between the two. He comes to a town called Sychar, near the field Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Jacob's well is there. And “Jesus, weary from His journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour” (verse 6). Hours were usually counted from sunrise, so this is about noon, in the heat of the day.

The Word who made all things (1:3) is tired and sits down. John does not hide it. The Word really did become flesh (1:14).
passages.hearers:
To a Jewish hearer, Samaria was not just a place on the road. It was an old wound.

The Samaritans worshipped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses. But they worshipped at their own mountain, Mount Gerizim, not at Jerusalem. The Jewish account of where they came from is in 2 Kings 17: after Assyria conquered the northern kingdom of Israel, it brought in people from other lands to live in the towns of Samaria (2 Kings 17:24). The Samaritans told their own story differently. They saw themselves as the true descendants of the northern tribes, the faithful keepers of the Law of Moses.

The bad feeling ran both ways and had a long history. After the exile, the Jewish leaders refused Samaritan help in rebuilding the temple (Ezra 4:3). Coins and other finds show that the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim around 111 or 110 BC. In Jesus' own lifetime, the Jewish historian Josephus says, some Samaritans slipped into the Jerusalem temple at Passover and scattered human bones there to defile it (Antiquities 18.29-30). He also tells of Galilean pilgrims killed at the village of Ginea on their way through Samaria (Antiquities 20.118).

So when John says Jesus ‘had to’ go through Samaria, hearers would feel it. And they should also know this: the Samaritans are not only people in an old story. A small Samaritan community still lives today, about nine hundred people, some in Holon near Tel Aviv and some at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim itself. They still keep their faith. The chapter that follows is about a Samaritan who is met with honour, and no reader should take from it any contempt for her people.
passages.ot: The place is full of Genesis. Jacob bought a plot of ground near Shechem “for a hundred pieces of silver” (Genesis 33:19). Later, “the bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the plot of land that Jacob had purchased” (Joshua 24:32). Jews and Samaritans both counted Jacob as their father. The well stood on ground both peoples remembered. The Old Testament does not tell the story of this well; the woman speaks of it as Jacob's gift (verse 12).
passages.hard: Why did Jesus ‘have to’ go through Samaria? One answer is simple geography. The road through Samaria was the shortest way from Judea to Galilee. But John uses the same Greek word, dei (‘must’), for what God's plan requires: ‘You must be born again’ (3:7), and the Son of Man ‘must be lifted up’ (3:14). So many readers hear a second meaning. Jesus had to go because someone was waiting at the well whom the Father meant him to meet. Both can be true at once. The road was short, and the meeting was planned.
passages.asks: Jesus walked straight into the place his people avoided, and he sat down there, tired. If you feel that you live in the wrong place, or that you belong to the wrong people, notice where he chose to rest. He is not too holy to be weary, and he is not too proud to sit on someone else's ground.

passages.happening:
A Samaritan woman comes to draw water. Jesus says to her, “Give Me a drink” (verse 7). His disciples have gone into town to buy food, so the two of them are alone.

She is astonished. “You are a Jew,” she says. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” John explains for his readers: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (verse 9).

Jesus answers with a riddle. If she knew the gift of God, and who was asking, she would have asked him, and he would have given her ‘living water’ (verse 10). She takes him literally. He has no bucket, and the well is deep. Is he greater than Jacob, who gave them this well? Jesus says that everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again. But the water he gives becomes “a fount of water springing up to eternal life” (verse 14). She says, “Sir, give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water” (verse 15). She still thinks he means water for a bucket.
passages.hearers:
Three things here would strike a first-century hearer.

First, he asks her for something. A Jewish teacher, alone with a woman he does not know, a Samaritan, asking to drink from her jar. Every line of custom said no. The Greek of John's little note in verse 9 may even be sharper than ‘do not associate’. A scholar named David Daube argued in 1950 that it means Jews do not use vessels in common with Samaritans, since a Samaritan's cup was thought to make a Jew ritually unclean. Some modern Bibles follow him. Others keep ‘associate with’, and some scholars question his reading of the Greek. Either way, Jesus is asking for the very cup custom forbade.

Second, ‘living water’ was an ordinary phrase. It meant running water, from a spring or a stream, as against still water stored in a cistern, a tank cut in rock to catch the rain. Living water was fresher and better. So the woman's mistake is a natural one.

Third, ‘Sir’ in verse 11 is the Greek word kurios. It is a polite word for a stranger, but it is also the word for ‘Lord’. She uses it without knowing how true it is. This is how John often tells a story: people say more than they know, and the reader is let in on the secret.
passages.ot: The prophets used ‘living water’ for God himself. Through Jeremiah God says, “They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water” (Jeremiah 2:13). Zechariah saw a day when “living water will flow out from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 14:8). And Isaiah joined water and the Spirit: “For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants” (Isaiah 44:3). Isaiah also called out, “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55:1). Later in John, Jesus will say plainly that the living water is the Spirit (7:37-39).
passages.asks: The woman wanted water so she would not have to keep walking to the well. Jesus offered her something that would not run dry. Many of us ask God for the smaller thing, the easier day, the full bucket. He does not mock that request. But he keeps offering more than we asked: himself, and a life with God that wells up from the inside.

passages.happening:
Suddenly Jesus changes direction. “Go, call your husband and come back” (verse 16). “I have no husband,” she says. Jesus answers, “You are correct to say that you have no husband. In fact, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband. You have spoken truthfully” (verses 17-18).

He knows her whole life, though they have just met. She sees it at once. “Sir,” she says, “I see that You are a prophet” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The text does not say why she had had five husbands. It is easy to fill the gap with a guess, and many preachers have. It is better to see first what a hearer in her world would know.

In her world a woman could not simply end a marriage. Under the Law of Moses, divorce was in the husband's hands: he could write her a certificate and send her away (Deuteronomy 24:1). A wife could be sent away for reasons that were no fault of hers, such as being unable to have children. Many women married young, and many were widowed young. The Law also had a custom called levirate marriage. When a man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). The Sadducees once asked Jesus about a woman married in turn to seven brothers (Luke 20:28-33). So death, divorce by a husband, and family custom could each pass one woman from marriage to marriage. Any of these, or several together, could lie behind her story. And the text does not say what kind of arrangement she has with the man she lives with now.

The noon hour has been used as evidence too. Some say she came at midday to avoid the other women because of her reputation. But the text does not say that either. A traveller resting at noon was normal, and people drew water when they needed it.
passages.ot: The woman calls Jesus a prophet, and for a Samaritan that word carried weight. Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses. In those books God promises, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). God adds, “I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18). A man who knows the hidden things of her life looks to her like that kind of prophet.
passages.hard:
Was the Samaritan woman an immoral woman? Christians have read her in two main ways.

The traditional reading, found in much preaching through the centuries, sees a woman whose life had gone badly wrong. Five husbands and a man who is not her husband look like a pattern of sin. Jesus brings it into the open, not to shame her but to heal her. Her change of subject to worship in verse 20 looks like someone turning away from a painful truth. And her later words, “He told me everything I ever did” (verse 39), sound like the relief of a person fully known and not thrown away.

Another reading sees a woman much wronged. Some scholars who study women in the ancient world point out that she may have been widowed more than once, or sent away by husbands, and that she had no power to end a marriage herself. On this reading, the man she lives with now may be someone she depends on, who would not or could not marry her. Readers who take this view notice what Jesus does not say. He does not call her a sinner. He does not tell her to repent. He tells her she has spoken the truth. And when she runs back to town, the people listen to her and come, which seems odd if everyone shunned her.

The text does not settle it, and these notes do not choose. What the text does say is clear. Jesus knows all of her story. He speaks of it plainly and without contempt. And he keeps talking with her. A few minutes later he tells her who he is.
passages.asks: If your own story holds more than one marriage, or a marriage that ended in grief, betrayal, or someone else's choice, notice how Jesus treats this woman. He knows everything. He says it without a single word of scorn. And then he does not walk away. Being fully known by him is not the end of the conversation. It is where the real conversation starts. If people in a church have shamed you for a past you could not control, this is not how Jesus spoke.

passages.happening:
The woman raises the great question between her people and his. “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem” (verse 20). ‘This mountain’ is Gerizim, which rises beside the old town of Shechem, near Sychar.

“Believe Me, woman,” Jesus answers, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (verse 21). Then he says something that does not flatter her: “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we do know, for salvation is from the Jews” (verse 22). And then: “But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (verse 23). “God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth” (verse 24).

She answers that the Messiah is coming, and when he comes he will explain everything. Jesus says, “I who speak to you am He” (verse 26). This is the first time in John's Gospel that Jesus plainly says he is the Messiah. He says it to a Samaritan woman at a well.
passages.hearers:
‘Woman’ in verse 21 was a polite way to speak to a woman, not a rude one. Jesus uses the same word for his mother (2:4).

The Samaritans hoped for a coming figure based on the prophet like Moses. In later Samaritan writings he is called the Taheb, a name usually explained as ‘the one who returns’ or ‘the Restorer’. How early that name was used is not certain. John gives her the word Messiah, and explains it for Greek readers: “called Christ” (verse 25).

Jesus' answer in verse 26 is, word for word in Greek, ‘I am, the one speaking to you’ (egō eimi). It can simply mean ‘I am he’. But John will use these two words again and again, and at times they seem to echo the way God names himself in the Old Testament. Scholars discuss which passages lie behind it. Here, at least, the plain sense is clear: the Messiah she is waiting for is the man asking her for a drink.
passages.ot: ‘Salvation is from the Jews’ rests on the oldest promise in the Bible. God told Abraham, “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The prophets pictured the nations streaming to Jerusalem: “For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3). But they also knew God could not be shut inside a building. Solomon prayed at the temple's opening, “Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (1 Kings 8:27). Jesus holds both truths together. God's saving work came through Israel. And it now reaches beyond any one mountain.
passages.hard:
Two lines in this passage are often misread.

The first is ‘salvation is from the Jews’ (verse 22). Some have heard it as a put-down of the Samaritans. Others, wanting to set Jesus against Judaism, have skipped over it. Both miss its weight. Jesus counts himself among the Jews: ‘we worship what we do know’. He says that God's way of saving the world came through Israel, through its covenants, its Scriptures and its prophets, and arrives now in a Jewish Messiah. Christians who forget this verse have sometimes spoken of the Jewish people with contempt. This verse forbids it. John's book page, in its part on ‘the Jews’ in John, points to this same verse.

The second is ‘in spirit and in truth’ (verse 24). Some have taken it to mean that only inner feeling matters, so that church buildings, ordered worship, the Lord's Supper and baptism do not. But Jesus is not setting the heart against the body. He is setting worship tied to one holy mountain against worship that the Spirit makes possible everywhere. Readers differ on ‘spirit’. Some take it to mean the human spirit, worship from the heart. Many take it to mean the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus has just described as wind and new birth (3:5-8). And ‘truth’ is a word John fills with Jesus himself: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6). Many readers hold both senses together: worship that comes from the heart, given by the Spirit, and shaped by the truth that Jesus is.
passages.asks: The woman tried to turn the talk to an old argument about places. Jesus did not wave it away, and he did not take her side either. He moved the question from where to whom. Many of us carry old arguments about the right church, the right style, the right side. This passage asks a quieter question: do you know the Father you are trying to worship, and have you met the one he sent?

passages.t: Come and see; fields ripe for harvest
passages.happening:
Just then the disciples come back. They are surprised that Jesus is talking with a woman, but no one asks him why (verse 27).

The woman leaves her water jar, goes into town, and says, “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” (verse 29). The people start out toward Jesus.

Meanwhile the disciples urge Jesus to eat. He says, “I have food to eat that you know nothing about” (verse 32). They wonder if someone brought him lunch. He explains: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work” (verse 34). Then he points at the fields. They say there are still four months until harvest. “I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest” (verse 35). Perhaps, as he speaks, the people of the town are already coming across those fields toward him.
passages.hearers:
The disciples' surprise had a reason. Many Jewish teachers were careful about speaking with women in public. The Mishnah, a book of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, keeps a saying from an early teacher, Yose ben Yohanan of Jerusalem, advising men not to talk much with women (Avot 1:5). It is a later book, and how far it reflects Jesus' day is not certain. But the disciples' surprise shows a caution of the same kind. Jesus has set it aside, and with a Samaritan.

She leaves her water jar. It is a small detail, and John chose to keep it. She came for water and goes back with news.

Her words to the town are careful: ‘Could this be the Christ?’ She does not preach. She tells what happened to her and asks a question. And she says, “a man who told me everything I ever did”. Whatever her past was, she is not hiding from it now. She uses it as her reason for hope.

The harvest saying would sound right to farmers. Grain was sown in the late autumn and reaped in the spring, months later. ‘Four months until harvest’ sounds like a saying for having to wait. Jesus says the waiting is over.
passages.ot: The prophets pictured a day of such plenty that harvest would never end: “the plowman will overtake the reaper” (Amos 9:13). Jesus says that day has come. The proverb in verse 37, ‘One sows and another reaps’, sounds like the curse in Micah: “You will sow but not reap” (Micah 6:15). In Jesus' hands it becomes good news. The one who sows and the one who reaps rejoice together (verse 36).
passages.hard: Who are the ‘others’ who did the hard work in verse 38? John does not say, and readers have given several answers. Some think of the prophets, and of John the Baptist, who prepared the way. Some think of Jesus himself, sowing in this conversation what the disciples will reap. Some think of the woman, whose testimony brings the town. Some think ahead to the book of Acts, where Philip preaches in a city of Samaria and the crowds listen gladly (Acts 8:5-6), and the apostles come after to share in the work. These answers can sit together. The point is plain: no one owns the harvest, and no worker starts from nothing.
passages.asks: The woman's witness was simple: come and see a man who knew me. She did not wait until she had answers to every question. If you think you know too little to speak about Jesus, notice that she knew only a little, and her town came. And if you are tired of work that seems to bear no fruit, verse 38 says that others sowed before you, and that someone after you may reap what you planted.

passages.happening:
Many Samaritans in the town believe in Jesus because of the woman's words. They ask him to stay, and he stays two days. A Jewish teacher is a guest in a Samaritan town.

Many more believe because of what he says to them himself. They tell the woman, “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world” (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
‘Savior’ was a title the Roman world knew well. Greek cities honoured Roman emperors as saviours. The scholar Craig Koester, in the Journal of Biblical Literature in 1990, showed that the phrase ‘savior of the world’ was used of emperors from Julius Caesar to Hadrian. In John, a village of despised Samaritans gives that title to a tired Jewish traveller. The whole world's true Saviour is not the man on the coins.

And Jesus stays. Two days as a guest, eating and sleeping under Samaritan roofs, in a town many of his people would not enter. No sermon in the chapter says it as loudly as that does.
passages.ot: The prophets said that God's servant would reach beyond Israel. God says to his servant in Isaiah, “It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob”, and then, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Through Isaiah God calls, “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22). The Samaritans' confession is that promise beginning to come true.
passages.asks: Faith often begins with someone else's words: a parent, a friend, a book. That is a good beginning. But the townspeople went further. They heard for themselves. If your faith so far rests mostly on what others have told you, this passage invites you to come close enough to hear him yourself, in the Gospels, in prayer, in the company of his people.

passages.t: The official's son, the second sign
passages.happening:
After two days Jesus goes on to Galilee. John adds a saying of Jesus: a prophet has no honour in his own home country (verse 44). Yet the Galileans welcome him, because they saw what he did at the feast in Jerusalem.

He comes again to Cana, where he turned water into wine. A royal official from Capernaum, whose son is dying, comes and begs Jesus to come down and heal him. Jesus says, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe” (verse 48). The father does not argue. “Sir,” he says, “come down before my child dies” (verse 49).

“Go,” said Jesus. “Your son will live.” And “the man took Jesus at His word and departed” (verse 50). On the way home his servants meet him: the boy is alive. He asks when he got better. “The fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour” (verse 52), about one in the afternoon. That was the very hour Jesus spoke. He and all his household believe. John counts this as Jesus' second sign (verse 54).
passages.hearers:
The official is called in Greek basilikos, a ‘king's man’. He was probably an officer serving Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee and whom people called king (Mark 6:14). A powerful man, then, but power could not keep his son alive.

Cana was in the hills; Capernaum was down on the shore of the lake, a long walk away. That is why he meets his servants on the road the next day.

Notice the steps in his faith. First he asks Jesus to come to the house. Then he believes the word alone and walks home without Jesus. Then, when he hears the hour, he and his whole household believe. Faith that starts small is still faith. In John's story it grows as Jesus' word proves true.

Jesus' sharp line in verse 48 is plural in Greek: ‘you people’. It is aimed at the crowd who want wonders, not only at this frightened father.
passages.ot: God's word heals at a distance in the Old Testament too: “He sent forth His word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20). And there is an echo of Elijah, who gave a dead boy back to his mother with the words, “Look, your son is alive” (1 Kings 17:23). In both stories a parent receives a child back by the word of God's servant. Here the word is spoken from miles away, and it is enough.
passages.hard:
Which ‘hometown’ is meant in verse 44? In the other Gospels the saying is about Nazareth (Mark 6:4; Luke 4:24). Here it is puzzling, because the Galileans welcome him. Some readers think John means Judea, the land of Jerusalem, where Jesus was born and where the leaders will reject him. Others think John means Galilee, and that the welcome is thin, since it rests on wonders, as verse 48 suggests. Both readings have defenders.

Is this the same story as the centurion's servant in Matthew 8:5-13 and Luke 7:1-10? Both are healings at a distance in Capernaum, at the word of Jesus, at a set hour. But the man here is a king's officer and the sick one is his son; there it is a centurion and his servant, and the conversation is different. Some think the Gospels tell one event in different ways; many think these were two events. These notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: This is a story for every parent who has sat beside a sick child. The father's faith was not strong. It was desperate, and Jesus still answered. But the story is not a promise that every prayer for healing will be answered the way we ask. Many faithful parents have prayed just as hard and buried a child. If that is your grief, you are not being told your faith failed. The weight of the story falls on Jesus' word, which has the last word over death, and on a Lord who met a frightened father on the road.
